Where it began

Ravi Bopara was born in Forest Gate, in East London, on 4 May 1985. He went to Brampton Manor and Barking Abbey schools, and learned much of his cricket at Frenford Clubs, playing for the Essex Boys and Girls Clubs side at under-14 level.

Essex gave him his first-class debut in May 2002. He played for England Under-19s in 2003 and 2004, including at the Under-19 World Cup, and in 2005 he made his first first-class hundred.

The player

He started as a top-order batsman and grew into an all-rounder in the shorter game, adding a handy line in medium pace. His one-day debut came early in 2007 and his first Test followed in Sri Lanka that December.

He played 13 Tests for England between 2007 and 2012, making 575 runs at 31.94 with three hundreds and a best of 143. Those three hundreds came one after another in 2009: 104 away against the West Indies, then 143 and another century at home against the same opponents. That made him only the fifth Englishman to score Test centuries in three straight innings. He gave the credit to Graham Gooch, who had coached him at Essex.

What made him special

In white-ball cricket he was the man England kept coming back to. He was part of the side that won the World Twenty20 in 2010, and in September 2011 he took 4 for 10, then the best return by any England bowler in a T20 international. His medium pace earned him a name as a partnership breaker, and in the 2013 Champions Trophy final he took 3 for 20.

He could also go big. In 2008 he hit an unbeaten 201 from 138 balls for Essex in a one-day quarter-final, only the eighth score of two hundred or more ever made in List A cricket.

Test cricket was a little less kind to him than one-day cricket was. His Test wickets column reads one, which is at least one more than many batsmen manage.

Away from the middle

He travelled the world with his bat. Among his teams were Kings XI Punjab in India, Sydney Sixers in Australia, Chittagong Vikings in Bangladesh and Karachi Kings in Pakistan's Super League. In 2016 he took over the Essex one-day captaincy, and that same year he captained Karachi Kings and was named player of the PSL, with 329 runs and 11 wickets. He later turned out for Northamptonshire, and from 2024 for Chitwan Rhinos in the Nepal Premier League.

And finally

In the first half of 2009 he could hardly stop making Test hundreds. Plenty of batsmen would settle for one spell like that in a whole career.
